stumbles.why: "They" is ambiguous, and so is the number of cells probed. 0.56% of the corpus is about 1/178, which is more than the 1/4096 (0.024%) that a single cell would hold. The reader can't work out how many cells are scanned.

stumbles.quote: I had expected the offset coding to be the win and the index cells to be a side note.
stumbles.why: This contradicts the earlier statement that the author expected faster training to be the payoff. It's unclear which expectation was real.

stumbles.quote: so the choice between the two algorithms comes down to training time
stumbles.why: This conflicts with the opening, where speed was the author's first expectation but is not presented as the main finding. The conclusion also quietly relies on e-means being faster, a point the text only supports for the benchmark above.

point: Using 4,096 k-means-style centroids (from Lloyd or the faster e-means) as index cells gave much better recall per amount scanned than remex's hash cells, which mattered more than the modest recall gain from offset coding or the training speedup.
